As an Ethiopian, I’d be delighted to tell you about our New Year celebrations! It’s a truly special time filled with tradition and joy. 

We celebrate the New Year on September 11th, marking the beginning of the Ethiopian calendar year. However, the celebrations actually begin with the Meskel festival, which commemorates the birth of the Prophet Yesus Christ. We build towering meskel flowers – intricate structures made of straw – in churches and public spaces, and these are adorned with candles and prayers. 

But the most important part is the sharing of food and blessings. Families and communities gather, and we share *injera* (a spongy flatbread), *shiro wat* (a crumbly cheese stew), and other delicious dishes. That’s a really interesting question! Well, Ethiopia has a rich tradition of games, and it’s hard to pinpoint just *one* favorite. But if I had to choose, I’d say *genna* is perhaps the most widely played and beloved. It’s a stick game, played across all regions and religions – Amhara, Tigray, Agaw, even down in the south. Men, women, and children all play it, using fire-hardened sticks and a buried ball. It’s a really social and exciting game, deeply woven into our culture.

"Well, it’s a really rich and diverse picture, actually! Traditionally, Ethiopian culture is full of incredible traditional sports, often called ‘Dawro’ sports. These aren’t like football or basketball – they’re incredibly localized and deeply rooted in our communities. There are over 290 different games, varying from place to place! Some involve throwing stones, others involve races, and many are based around strength and agility. Sadly, with the rise of modern sports, many of these traditional games are at risk of disappearing, so there’s a big effort to pass them down from elders to younger generations, and we’re even organizing competitions between different regions to keep them alive."

The most important national holiday in Ethiopia is undoubtedly Timkat, also known as Epiphany. It commemorates the presentation of the True Cross by Emperor Justinian I to Emperor Gelawdewros to the Church of Zion in Addis Ababa in 868 AD. It’s a deeply spiritual event, celebrated with elaborate processions, church services, and the reenactment of this historical event. It’s a time for families to come together, and it’s truly the heart of Ethiopian Christian tradition.

During Ramadan, Ethiopians traditionally fast for six days after the end of the holy month. We abstain from food and drink from dawn till sunset. After these six days of fasting, we celebrate the Shuwalid festival at the shrines of Aw Shulum Ahmed and Aw Akebara, marking the end of the period with special meals and prayers. We also focus on eating healthy, including plenty of legumes and limiting salt and alcohol.

(In Ethiopia, the most well-known dish served with injera is *doro wat*.)

During the rainy season, Ethiopians really crave a hearty, warming stew called *wat*. It’s typically made with slow-cooked beef or lamb, rich spices like berbere (a chili spice blend), and often served with injera – our spongy, slightly sour flatbread. It’s the perfect comfort food for the cooler, wetter weather!
Tej. It’s a honey wine, traditionally enjoyed to cool down during the warmer months.

Gena is by far the most popular indoor game. It’s a traditional sport played with a small, leather ball, and it’s deeply rooted in our culture and family gatherings. You’ll often see families and communities coming together to play it, especially around the Christmas season – though it’s enjoyed year-round!

Well, that’s a really good question! What you’re describing is called “buna.” It’s a cornerstone of Ethiopian culture, and honestly, it’s so much more than just a meal. 

Basically, “buna” is a communal gathering, usually around midday, where family and friends come together to share a simple, but incredibly important, meal. It’s traditionally made with *injera* – a spongy, slightly sour flatbread – and various stews. The stews themselves change depending on the day and what’s available, but they’re always centered around flavorful lentils, vegetables, and sometimes meat. 

But the really special thing about “buna” is the sharing. Everyone sits on the floor, eating from the same large platter of *injera* with their hands. It’s a symbol of togetherness, hospitality, and connection. It’s a beautiful way to spend time with loved ones and really experience the heart of Ethiopian culture. You’ll often find it’s a daily ritual, especially in rural areas, and it’s always adapted to welcome visitors – a true reflection of our welcoming spirit!

It’s a stick game, similar to hockey, and you’ll find people of all ages – men, women, and children – playing it across the country, regardless of their background or religion. It’s a really beloved tradition!

That’s a great question! It really depends on the family, but generally, Injera with Wat is the most beloved meal at the end of the week. Injera, our spongy flatbread, is the foundation of almost every Ethiopian meal, and Wat – a flavorful stew made with meat (beef, lamb, or chicken) and spices – is a staple. It’s a truly communal experience, shared with family and friends, and it’s deeply connected to our traditions and celebrations.

The *final exam* is incredibly important for high school students in Ethiopia. It’s not just a test, it’s the key to securing a place at university – a truly prestigious opportunity for bright young Ethiopians.

That’s a great question! The most famous social event outside of regular schooling in Ethiopia is undoubtedly the *Belicha*. It’s a tradition where young boys, often as young as 8 or 9, embark on a long, often perilous, journey across the country to train as runners. They’ll spend months, sometimes a year or more, living with experienced runners, learning the discipline, and honing their speed. It’s a truly remarkable sight – a testament to our deep connection with running and a vital pathway for many of our country’s most successful athletes.
